title: Sysmon
summary: Sysmon, short for System Monitor, is a Microsoft Windows service and kernel driver that writes detailed events about process creation, network connections, image and driver loading, and selected file and registry changes into the Windows event log. It extends the default Windows auditing, which records far less about process behaviour, and because it runs as a driver it can attach a process identifier and globally unique process tag so related events can be correlated across a session. In real environments it is a primary telemetry source for endpoint detection and response platforms and for detection rules written in query languages such as Sigma. The mistake people make is installing it and expecting value from the defaults: the shipped configuration is deliberately conservative, and useful detail comes from a tuned configuration whose noisy event types are filtered to suit the environment. Without a pipeline that centralises and retains the events, the log is rarely read at all.

beginner.definition: Sysmon is a free tool from Microsoft that watches what happens on a Windows computer. It records events such as programs starting and network connections opening. Those records are written into the Windows event log. Security teams then search that log to find suspicious activity.
beginner.whyItMatters: Windows keeps some records by itself, but they are often too thin to explain an attack. Sysmon adds detail such as which program started another program and which network address it contacted. Without that detail, investigators cannot tell a normal update from harmful activity. Good records also help you answer what happened after an incident has ended. If those records are missing, you may never learn how far an intruder reached.
howItWorks: You install Sysmon as a service and a driver on each Windows computer you want to watch.
The driver observes activity such as a new program starting or a network connection opening.
Each event is written to the Windows event log with an event number and a process identifier.
A configuration file decides which events are kept and which noisy ones are ignored.
A central agent forwards the events to a security platform for searching and alerting.
Analysts then write rules against those events to detect behaviour that looks suspicious.
beginner.example: Imagine a night security guard in a large office block. The building already has door alarms, but they only report that a door opened. The guard writes a short note for every door, lift and delivery, and records who arrived with whom. Later, when a theft is reported, those notes show the full route through the building. Sysmon is that guard for a Windows computer, and the event log is the notebook.
takeaways: Sysmon adds rich Windows activity records that normal auditing does not provide.
The configuration file is what makes it useful, because the defaults are limited and noisy rules must be filtered.
Events are only valuable when they are forwarded to a central place and somebody reviews them.

objectives: Explain what Sysmon is and which Windows activity it records.
Describe why default Windows auditing is often insufficient for an investigation.
Identify the role of the Sysmon configuration file in tuning event collection.
Explain how process identifiers let analysts link related events.
Describe how endpoint telemetry reaches a central detection platform.
Recognise the operational work needed to keep endpoint logging useful.
